text:
A federal judge appointed by former President Joe Biden told the Trump administration Tuesday that it needs to stop its sweeping arrests of immigrants in court, saying the government failed to justify broad changes that expanded arrests at courthouses and prolonged detention times.

The Trump administration drastically ramped up arrests of suspected illegal immigrants at Department of Justice (DOJ) immigration courts after President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, sparking criticism from attorneys and lawmakers that immigrants going through the proper legal channels were being unfairly targeted. At the same time, those who were detained were held for longer periods, after a 12-hour cap was lifted.

In a 71-page order, U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts found that policies introduced by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the DOJ's immigration court system violated federal administrative law because they were adopted without adequate explanation or consideration of their impact.

Read More on Politics

"For 80 years, Congress has commanded federal agencies to think before they act," Pitts wrote, referring to the Administrative Procedures Act (APA) meant to govern how policies are changed.

"Because the record before the Court demonstrates that ICE and EOIR [Executive Office of Immigration Review] failed to provide reasoned explanations for their actions, the Court concludes that each of the challenged policies is arbitrary and capricious in contravention of the APA," the judge said.

The court blocked the policies nationwide, delivering a significant setback to the administration’s broader effort to ramp up immigration enforcement.

"In sum, ICE’s 2025 courthouse-arrest policies are devoid of rational explanation," Pitts said.

In response to the ruling, Department of Homeland Security (DHS) General Counsel James Percival told Newsweek, "When a judge sentences a defendant, the defendant is taken into custody. If an alien is ordered removed by an immigration judge, the same should happen. A district judge ordering otherwise is naked judicial activism in service of an anti-American, open borders agenda."

What the Judge Found

The case centered on whether federal agencies properly justified sweeping changes to immigration enforcement in 2025.

Pitts made clear that the issue was not whether the government could enforce immigration law, but whether it followed the rules when changing policy.

When talking about the APA, Pitts said that the law requires agencies to "provide sound reasons for following [their] chosen course."

Instead, the court found ICE and its partner agency failed to meet that basic standard, concluding they "failed to provide reasoned explanations for their actions."

The ruling builds directly on a March admission by the Trump administration that it had relied on a flawed legal justification for courthouse arrests, using guidance that "does not and has never applied" to immigration courts.

Detention Expansion Also Struck Down

The ruling also invalidated a separate ICE policy allowing migrants to be held in short-term holding facilities for up to 72 hours in lieu of the long-standing 12-hour limit. The court also found major flaws in how the policy was adopted.

The agency failed to consider "important aspects of the problem," including risks tied to detention conditions and whether alternatives—such as reducing arrests—were available, the judge wrote.

The opinion also highlighted inconsistencies in the government’s approach, saying that "an unexplained inconsistency in agency policy" is itself grounds for finding a rule unlawful.

Immediate Impact of the Ruling

The decision means the policies are no longer in effect nationwide.

Under federal law, courts reviewing agency action must "set aside" policies found to be unlawful, the judge ruled, ordering full vacatur rather than limiting relief to the plaintiffs in the case. Vacatur effectively annuls a previous judgment or proceeding.

As a result:

ICE no longer has authority to broadly conduct courthouse arrests under the 2025 guidance.

The 72-hour detention rule is invalidated.

Earlier restrictions on enforcement and detention may effectively be reinstated.

The ruling does not prohibit ICE from making arrests at courthouses entirely, but requires that any such policies be backed by a reasoned explanation.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court sided with the Trump administration Tuesday in an immigration case dealing with the government’s power over green card holders accused of crimes.

The 6-3 decision centers on an immigration officers’ 2012 decision to put lawful permanent resident Muk Choi Lau on immigration parole when he returned from a short trip to China because he had been accused of a counterfeiting crime.

Lau argued that the officer overstepped their authority, and the decision wrongly allowed the Department of Homeland Security under then-President Barack Obama an easier path to removal after he pleaded guilty to selling counterfeit clothes in New Jersey.

The high court disagreed. “Border officers did not have the burden to establish by clear and convincing evidence that Lau had committed a crime involving moral turpitude,” Justice Clarence Thomas wrote in the opinion.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented, writing that the decision to put Lau on immigration parole effectively sentenced him to “immigration limbo” before he’d been convicted of any crime.

“I worry that the Court has now handed the Government a massive blank check,” she wrote in the dissent joined by her two liberal colleagues.

The liberal group Alliance for Justice echoed that concern, saying the ruling could provide an expanded path for revoking green cards.

But Advancing American Freedom, a group founded by former Republican Vice President Mike Pence, called it an important case to allow the removal of people who “abuse the privilege of being granted lawful permanent resident status.”

The decision comes as the high court considers a series of immigration-related issues against the backdrop of President Donald Trump’s sweeping immigration crackdown, though this case started before Trump took office.

His administration argued that suspicion of a crime is enough to put a lawful permanent resident, also known as a green-card holder, on immigration parole. Federal attorneys urged the court to take an expansive view of executive authority over immigration.

text:
In June 2026, two federal court decisions created potential implications for employers sponsoring foreign national employees and individuals with pending immigration benefit applications. Although the cases involve different USCIS policies and arise from separate legal challenges, both have immediate operational implications and underscore the uncertainty that ongoing immigration litigation can create for employers.

Rhode Island Court Vacates USCIS Adjudication Policies

A federal court vacated several USCIS policy directives that affected how the agency reviewed and processed certain immigration benefit requests.

On June 5, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island issued an order vacating three USCIS policy issuances:

Policy Memorandum PM 602-0192

Policy Memorandum PM 602-0194

Policy Alert PA 2025-26

The court found that the challenged policies introduced substantive changes to adjudication and case-processing procedures without following the administrative requirements necessary to implement them. Based on those findings, the court concluded that the policies violated the Administrative Procedure Act and could not remain in effect.

The policies affected internal USCIS adjudication procedures and case processing practices. Among other things, they provided for:

Adjudication holds for certain immigration benefit requests;

Additional review or re-review of pending and previously adjudicated matters; and

Increased discretionary scrutiny relating to certain categories or factors.

In practical terms, these policies contributed to longer processing times across several immigration filing categories, including employment-based petitions. Because the court vacated the policies, USCIS must now treat them as having no force or effect.

For the time being, USCIS officers are expected to adjudicate cases under existing statutory authority, applicable regulations, and guidance that was in place before these policies were issued.

For employers whose cases were delayed or placed on hold under these policies, the court’s decision may allow those matters to resume normal processing. Employers should promptly identify any affected cases and work with immigration counsel to evaluate whether follow-up with USCIS is appropriate to help ensure those matters are returned to active adjudication. Given that USCIS has stated it disagrees with the Rhode Island court’s ruling, while confirming it will comply with the order as it considers potential next steps, employers should take a proactive approach to monitoring impacted cases and seeking updates where necessary.

Updates to the $100,000 H-1B Proclamation Fee

A federal district court in Massachusetts initially ruled that the $100,000 H-1B fee policy was unlawful and ordered that it be vacated nationwide. The court concluded that the fee functioned as a tax and that the executive branch lacked authority to impose it through a presidential proclamation. The court also found that the policy exceeded statutory authority and failed to comply with the Administrative Procedure Act.

The government promptly appealed that decision. The Massachusetts court subsequently paused the effect of its vacatur order while the appellate process moves forward. As a result, USCIS may continue requiring the $100,000 fee for H-1B petitions that seek, or are eligible only for, consular notification rather than change-of-status approval.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit will decide whether USCIS may continue collecting the fee while the appeal is pending.

At present, employers should recognize that the fee’s future remains uncertain. Depending on the appellate court’s ruling, the fee could be suspended again, remain in effect during the appeal, or become subject to further court orders. Employers considering H-1B filings that may be affected by the fee should carefully assess timing, budget considerations, and filing strategy with counsel.

Practical Implications for Employers

Both decisions are significant, but neither issue appears fully resolved. Additional court rulings and agency guidance are expected in the coming weeks and months.

Employers, foreign nationals, and sponsoring organizations should proactively review pending matters, anticipated filings, and any planned travel or consular processing to account for current requirements, possible fee obligations, processing delays, and further changes. Given the pace of recent developments, close attention to future agency announcements and court decisions will remain important.

text:
A federal judge in California has issued a ruling banning Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents from making arrests inside immigration courts nationwide, blocking one of the Trump administration’s strategies for carrying out mass deportations.

When the Trump administration began its crackdown on illegal immigration last year, ICE reversed its previous guidance against making arrests in or near immigration courthouses.

As a result, many people accused of being in the country illegally have been detained and separated from their families when they show up for routine immigration hearings and check-ins.

In Los Angeles, the policy shift led to sweeping arrests at immigration courts, including a teenager who was detained a day after he graduated high school with honors and a father handcuffed in front of his 8-year-old son moments after a judge issued a dismissal of his deportation case.

Immigration attorneys have spoken out against the practice, saying it punishes people who are trying to comply with the rules and turns the justice system into a place of fear. The Department of Homeland Security has argued that courts are a safe and convenient place to detain people who are in the country illegally.

On Tuesday, Judge P. Casey Pitts, with the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, issued a 71-page ruling calling the practice “arbitrary and capricious” and saying that it conflicted with prior concerns ICE had raised about the negative effect courthouse arrests have on attendance rates. Pitts was nominated to the federal bench by President Biden.

“The policies entirely fail to address the chilling effect of courthouse arrests on noncitizens’ attendance at court proceedings, which is both a critical factor underlying ICE’s 2021 guidance and an ‘important aspect of the problem’ in its own right,” Pitts wrote.

James Percival, the general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security, decried the ruling in a statement on X, calling it “naked judicial activism in service of an anti-American, open borders agenda.”

“When a judge sentences a defendant, the defendant is taken into custody,” Percival wrote. “If an alien is ordered removed by an immigration judge, the same should happen.”

Attorney Gene Hamilton, who played a key role in ending Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals while working in the Justice Department during Trump’s first term, lambasted the ruling as lawless.

“ICE can’t arrest illegal aliens at immigration court?” he wrote in a statement on X. “Won’t last on appeal. But more insanity intended to eliminate immigration enforcement.”

The ruling was issued as part of a class-action lawsuit filed by noncitizens challenging ICE’s recent practice of making arrests at immigration courthouses and detaining people for extended periods in facilities designed for short-term holds.

The case was initiated in August by an asylum-seeker from Guatemala who was arrested after leaving a routine immigration hearing in San Francisco and then held without access to adequate hygiene, sanitation, medical care and legal advice, according to the complaint.

Tuesday’s ruling follows a similar decision issued by Pitts in November that more narrowly restricted ICE from making arrests at immigration courthouses across Northern California, which he said made noncitizens face a choice between “two irreparable harms.”

“First, they may appear in immigration court and face likely arrest and detention,” he wrote in December. “Alternatively, noncitizens may choose not to appear and instead to forego their opportunity to pursue their claims for asylum or other relief from removal.”

Most people who do not show up for court hearings are ordered removed in absentia. The number of such orders issued sharply increased from around 19,000 in fiscal year 2024 to more than 50,000 in fiscal year 2025, according to Justice Department data.

Last month, a federal judge issued a ruling largely barring ICE from making such arrests at immigration courthouses in New York City.

On Tuesday, Democratic New Jersey Congresswoman Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman called on Congress to codify Pitt’s latest ruling into law by passing a bill that would ban federal agents from arresting people who show up to have their immigration cases reviewed.

“Immigrants attempting to follow immigration laws should not be punished for their good faith efforts,” she said in a statement. “The systematic arrest of immigrants attending court hearings and other appointments related to their status violates fundamental values of fairness.”

text:
Dear Friend,

I want to bring to your attention the horrific atrocities happening inside ICE's immigrant detention camps. Children are going sick and hungry. Neglected by detention staff, people with life-threatening illnesses are dying in squalid living conditions. Time and again, we've heard stories of abhorrent human rights abuses, and the Department of Justice just published a scathing report detailing the cruel and inhumane treatment of detainees in California's privately-run, for-profit detention facilities.

Corporations are profiting from human suffering by doing business with ICE. As the federal regime continues its mass detention campaign, ICE has opened California's 8th detention facility, with plans to build another detention center in Santa Clara County. More kidnappings mean more profit for ICE's corporate collaborators.

Read on: Assembly approves several bills

aimed at regulating ICE - CapRadio

We're meeting the moment with fierce urgency at the State Assembly. My bill, the No Tax Breaks For ICE Contractors Act, just passed the Assembly Floor to cancel tax credits for companies that contract with the Department of Homeland Security and its immigration enforcement agencies. Taxpayer dollars should not be used to subsidize corporations that aid and abet ICE's reckless violence. With ICE rapidly expanding its detention system, I have also proposed legislation to increase public oversight of the approval of any new immigration detention centers.

My legislation is part of the State Assembly's concerted efforts to protect our immigrant families. We are doing everything we can to obstruct ICE by passing legislation to tax private detention centers, protect polling stations and day care facilities from ICE agents, and prohibit them from ever becoming public employees who are paid with our state's taxpayer dollars. You can see here for more about our work to counter ICE.

Legislation Passes the Assembly

I am proud that 10 of my bills are headed to the Senate after passing the State Assembly. Beyond my work in fighting against ICE's terror campaign, I am focused on tackling the housing crisis, advancing the state's climate goals, empowering our workers, and more.

Immigrant protection

AB 1675 - The No Tax Breaks for ICE Contractors Act

The bill ensures that California does not spend taxpayer dollars to bankroll corporations that aid and abet ICE's indiscriminate violence.

AB 1801 - Public Notice for Private Detention Centers

The bill increases public oversight of immigration detention centers by ensuring that people have adequate time to organize and voice their concerns before their local government approves any new contracts with detention facilities.

Housing

AB 1997 - Expedite Affordable Housing Construction

The bill accelerates affordable housing construction by speeding up the approval of housing developments that are 90% affordable to very-low or extremely-low income households.

AB 2601 - Accelerate Smaller Housing Developments

The bill creates a more efficient review process for condominium projects, accessory dwelling units (ADUs), and other smaller-scale residential housing, which will expedite the development of housing units.

Worker Empowerment

AB 1729 - State Telework

The bill empowers and supports our state workers by ensuring transparency about their agency's telework policy.

AB 1916 - Collective Bargaining for ASL Interpreters

The bill strengthens language access in California courts and supports the court interpreter workforce. It allows American Sign Language (ASL) interpreters working in California's trial courts to participate in the same collective bargaining process as other certified court interpreters.

Animal Welfare & Veterinary Care

AB 1733 - Continuing Education for Veterinarians

The bill expands communities' access to spay/neuter services and encourages veterinarians to volunteer for animal shelters. It modernizes California's veterinary continuing education requirements by creating a dedicated continuing education pathway, which recognizes up to 4 hours of free spay/neuter services delivered to shelters and rescue organizations.

Sustainable Transit

AB 1944 - Zero-Emission Buses

The bill provides California transit agencies with the flexibility needed to continue their transition to zero-emission fleets.

Education

AB 1763 - Excused Absences for Religious Observance

The bill enables students to be excused from school without administrators' approval to observe a holiday or ceremony for their religion, which protects them from losing academic credits.

Health care

AB 1949 - Medi-Cal Coverage for Acupuncture

The bill expands access to acupuncture for Medi-Cal patients by allowing patients to access up to 24 acupuncture visits per year.

Pride on the Alameda - June 27

In celebration of Pride Month in June, I'm excited to co-host the resource fair "Pride on the Alameda." Come join us on Saturday, June 27 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the Billy DeFrank LGBTQ+ Community Center in San Jose!

Government agencies and community organizations will share LGBTQ+ health and wellness resources, such as HIV testing information and mental health services. Pride on the Alameda will also celebrate the 45th anniversary of the Billy DeFrank LGBTQ+ Community Center. Thank you to the center, along with San Jose Councilmember Anthony Tordillos and the Santa Clara County Office of LGBTQ Affairs, for co-hosting the event.

I look forward to seeing you here!

Youth Art Contest Winners

(Recognizing our Youth Art Contest winners at the State Assembly)

Congratulations to the winners of my 2026 Youth Art Contest! I had the opportunity to recognize our winners at the State Assembly, and their talents in illustrating the theme Healthy Meals Feed Happy Families were impressive. Their artistic vision of food serving as a foundation of a healthy community is inspiring, and I'm honored to display their artwork in my Capitol Office over the year!

(Winning artwork of the 2026 Youth Art Contest)

Asian American and Pacific Islander Month Volunteer Opportunity

(Volunteering at Loaves and Fishes for Asian American

and Pacific Islander Month)

In recognition of Asian American and Pacific Islander Month in May, I joined Loaves and Fishes to give back and support our neighbors. Together, we prepared over 3,000 fresh, nutritious meals for those in need. Thank you to our volunteers who generously gave their time. Your service to our community makes a real difference, and I hope to see you in future volunteer opportunities.

A special thank you to Berryessa Boardmember Jai Srinivasan and Newark Councilmember Eve Marie Little for joining us.

One of the most devastating federal policy changes to CalFresh, federally known as SNAP, has taken effect. Starting June 1, 2026, the Republican budget bill, H.R. 1, imposes cruel and punitive work requirements to cut off vital food aid from low-income families. Over half a million people statewide are at risk of losing their CalFresh benefits.

The federal policy subjects people to bureaucratic paperwork designed as red tape traps. 8.8 million Californians are already struggling with food insecurity, and the new work requirements will force even more people into hunger and poverty.

"California taxpayers have contributed tens of billions of dollars more than we receive from Washington, yet we're left holding the bill and bearing the harm." - Assemblymember Alex Lee, ABC 7 news

During this time of urgent need, I wanted to share some resources to help you navigate the policy changes as best you can. Here is a list of organizations that distribute food to our communities:

Alameda County Community Food Bank

Catholic Charities of Santa Clara County

Hunger at Home

Loaves and Fishes

Second Harvest of Silicon Valley

SOS Meals on Wheels

TCV Food Bank & Mobile Pantry

For those who have the means to help, consider volunteering at food banks or other organizations that assist families in need. Now is the time for us to step up for one another.

Sincerely,

text:
A federal appeals court on Tuesday allowed the Trump administration to move forward with an effort to expand fast-track deportations throughout the U.S., in a legal win for the president's crackdown on illegal immigration.

The 2-1 decision by a panel of judges at the U.S. Circuit Court for the District of Columbia Circuit allows the Department of Homeland Security to carry out an expansion of the expedited removal process, which empowers federal immigration officials to deport some detainees without court hearings.

Before the second Trump administration, the expedited removal policy was limited to areas close to the border and only applied to recent entrants who could not prove they had been living in the country for more than two weeks.

But the policy allowed to take effect Tuesday — which was drafted in the first week of President Trump's second term in January 2025 — expands expedited removal to anywhere in the United States. Officials can use it on any unauthorized immigrant who cannot prove they have been in the country for more than two years.

In August 2025, a federal judge found the Trump administration's expansion of expedited removal violated due process rights, following a lawsuit from immigrant advocacy group Make the Road New York. The panel of appellate judges disagreed Tuesday, invalidating her order.

The two appellate judges in the majority — Trump-appointed Justin Walker and Neomi Rao — found the policy offers sufficient due process protections.

"Make the Road has not shown that the expedited-removal process denies its members notice and an opportunity to be heard," they wrote.

Last August, a lower court judge called the government's procedures for ensuring people aren't accidentally subjected to expedited removal "woefully inadequate," writing that migrants were not even informed of the fact that being in the country for at least two years is a possible defense. On Tuesday, the appellate court pushed back, finding that standard "would require immigration officers to provide what amounts to legal advice."

Obama-appointed Circuit Judge Robert Wilkins dissented from the core of the ruling, arguing the policy deprives people of due process rights. In part, he wrote that the policy doesn't require immigration officials to ask migrants how long they have been in the country, or inform them of the two-year rule.

"Absent such knowledge, the noncitizen is simply left to hope that the immigration officer will conclude that they have met their burden of demonstrating two-years of continuous presence at the initial screening interview," Wilkins wrote.

James Percival, the top lawyer at DHS, said Tuesday's order "vindicated our decision to apply the law as written."

"It's not too late to take a $2,600 check and a free flight home!" Percival added, referring to the Trump administration's incentives to push people in the U.S. illegally to self-deport.

Anand Balakrishnan, senior staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union and lead counsel in the lawsuit over the expedited removal policy, said the group is "exploring next steps."

"The Trump administration's push for fast-track deportations will subject people to an unfair and error-prone system," Balakrishnan said in a statement. "This ruling undermines the fundamental principle that people receive due process when the government seeks to deport them."

Make the Road New York Deputy Director Yaritza Mendez said in a statement: "The Trump administration's attempt to expand expedited removal is just one of the many attacks that immigrant communities face daily. If allowed to move forward, it would severely undermine due process and lead to countless unjust or wrongful deportations, irreparably tearing apart families forever."

The expansion of expedited removal is part of a series of Trump administration policies designed to surge deportations by speeding up the process. Last month, the government hired its largest-ever class of immigration judges, onboarding dozens of judges after pushing out more than 100, some of whom allege they were fired for not backing mass deportations.

text:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection is one of the premiere revenue collection agencies in the world. Above, CBP Import Specialist Omar Madrigal examines a shipment of pineapples at the Pharr Texas Port of Entry to see if the produce qualifies for entry under a free trade agreement. CBP photo by Roderick Kise

Early last year when U.S. Customs and Border Protection collected $34 million from a major consumer products company for falsely using a free trade agreement, the agency proved its expertise in revenue collection. The goods, electronic household devices, were assembled and shipped from Mexico, but the component parts were from China and still subject to duties. Although the evasion technique is a relatively new one, CBP’s mastery in revenue collection is not.

For 236 years, since the U.S. Customs Service, one of CBP’s legacy agencies, was created as the Fifth Act of Congress in 1789, the agency has been collecting revenue for the U.S. During its first year of operation, U.S. Customs produced more than $2 million in revenue. For the next 125 years, until income tax legislation passed in 1913, duties collected by the U.S. Customs Service were the economic engine of the country, financing virtually the entire government and its infrastructure.

As the main source of income for the young nation, customs duties funded a number of projects of historical significance. These included paying off the Revolutionary War debt, financing the Louisiana Purchase, acquiring the Oregon territories and the states of Florida and Alaska. Duties also financed the Lewis and Clark Expedition, the building of the U.S. Naval and Military Academies, the transcontinental railroad, and the city of Washington, D.C. Fast forward to today — in fiscal year 2025, CBP collected over $216 billion in total trade revenue, reinforcing its position as one of the federal government’s top revenue-generating agencies, second only to the Internal Revenue Service.

When the electronic household devices were imported into the U.S., the country of origin was initially declared as China on the shipping documents. The consumer products company importing the goods paid the required duties, but then filed a correction on the shipments, changing the country of origin to Mexico. This meant the electronic devices would fall under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement, making the products duty free. The importer wanted a refund and to bring in future shipments of the devices duty free.

Although importers are allowed to correct errors for a specified window of time, CBP flagged the shipment for a document review. “Changing the country of origin on goods is significant and requires substantial information to change it from the original declaration,” said Mary Freeman, the supervisory import specialist at CBP’s Consumer Products and Mass Merchandising Center who was part of the team that conducted the review. “You can’t just say, ‘Oh, the country of origin is really Mexico, not China. Take our word for it.’”

CBP requested more information from the importer about the devices, but that led to more questions. “One of the photos the company sent showed that the product was marked ‘Made in China,’” said Omar Madrigal, the CBP import specialist who was reviewing the documents. “That raised a red flag.” So Madrigal asked the importer for more information. He researched the raw materials that were used in the finished product and looked at the rules of origin with his supervisor. “What makes something a product of China or a product of Mexico? Some of the rules of origin are simple, some not so much,” said Freeman, who reached out to one of CBP’s national import specialists who specializes in commodities. The national import specialist determined that the product had not been substantially transformed and that the consumer products company owed additional duties, not less.

“An easy analogy,” said Freeman, “is if you have wheat flour from Italy and you ship it to Mexico and turn it into spaghetti, is the spaghetti from Mexico or Italy? The wheat came from Italy, but it changed from flour to spaghetti, which is a substantial transformation. The flour became spaghetti in Mexico, so it’s Mexican spaghetti,” she said. However, this was not the case for the electronic devices. “The devices were assembled in Mexico with components that were manufactured in China,” Freeman said. “The components had not undergone any substantial transformation to create the final product.”

“CBP is fair and reasonable in our enforcement of tariffs and trade. If a company makes a mistake and takes responsibility for it, we don’t go after them and cut them off at the knees and charge them penalties,” said Lori Whitehurst, the director of trade operations for CBP’s Office of Field Operations. “We recognize that people make mistakes. We get that, but there are others who are illicitly trying to evade duties. Those are the ones that we go after. They are high-risk companies in terms of revenue loss. They undermine U.S. domestic industry and threaten our economic security.”

Perfected expertise

CBP has perfected its expertise in revenue collection as the trade landscape has evolved. “We’ve been agile and we pay attention to the trade trends,” said Whitehurst. “But just as our methods of duty collection have become more sophisticated so have the schemes of duty evasion.”

The import process is complex and lengthy. “It doesn’t happen in a day. It starts when goods are shipped from a foreign country, and as the cargo travels to the U.S., we’re gathering data on what’s coming,” said Whitehurst. “The first point that we can intercept shipments evading duties is at the ports of entry where CBP officers can detain cargo and physically examine the contents.”

The officers rely on input from import specialists and entry specialists who are part of CBP’s 10 industry-specific Centers of Excellence and Expertise, which are based throughout the country. “The Centers of Excellence and Expertise include the principal people who perform revenue collection for the agency,” said Melvin Moreland, director of CBP’s Consumer Products and Mass Merchandising Center. “We’re the ones who issue the bills, issue the penalties, and determine the duties. We’re primarily responsible for ensuring the correct duty amounts are assessed and collected.”

The import specialists and entry specialists physically sit alongside the officers at the ports, but they have national authority, so they can impact the flow of cargo at any port of entry. “If we find an importer who is doing something nefarious in New York, the Centers can penalize that importer and target shipments across all of the ports of entry,” said Whitehurst. “We know that if an importer is doing something illegal in New York, they’re probably doing it in Miami, Los Angeles, or other ports.”

CBP also has a very sophisticated automated cargo processing system. “It’s a tool in our toolbox that we use to target, identify risk areas and uncover schemes,” said Whitehurst. “So we have many different resources within CBP that we use to protect the nation’s revenue. This is what makes us extremely successful in what we do and positions us as one of the premiere revenue collection agencies in the world.”

Additionally, CBP enforces regulations for nearly 50 different federal government agencies. “We make sure that the duties, taxes, and fees are collected properly for these agencies as well,” said Moreland. Furthermore, CBP is the primary agency with border search authority. “We have the ability to search to find out if the right duties are being collected and submitted by importers. Most agencies don’t have border search authority. They might have some regulatory border authority. For example, the Consumer Products Safety Commission, FDA, and USDA have regulatory authorities on the border, but CBP is the frontline agency that has border search authority for everything coming into the country including people and goods.”

CBP’s Consumer Products and Mass Merchandising Center Director Melvin Moreland, right, consults CBP Import Specialist Jamelia Akita at the Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport to determine if a shipment of jewelry qualifies for duty-free treatment. CBP photo by Brian Walker

Evasion schemes

Importers try to evade duties in multiple ways. A common way is to undervalue goods. For example, in August 2025, three shipments containing 12 watches arrived at the Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport via an express courier service. The declared value of the watches was approximately $500 each, but an astute CBP officer suspected that the watches were worth more and detained the shipments. The officer consulted a CBP import specialist who contacted the manufacturer to determine the real value.

“These were very, very expensive Swiss Patek Philippe designer watches that were valued at over $1.9 million,” said Paul Sumbi, assistant director of the enforcement division of CBP’s Consumer Products and Mass Merchandising Center. “The watches were shipped from St. Maarten in the Caribbean. The seller undervalued them to evade duties.”

The buyer, who imported the 12 watches, paid $21,000 in duties to retrieve his merchandise. Sumbi and his team also researched how many times the buyer had imported designer watches in the past and calculated the amount of his unpaid duties. “It resulted in a loss of revenue of over $86,740 for his previous shipments, which we are now in the process of collecting,” said Sumbi. “On top of that, we issued him a penalty of $108,000.”

Misclassification is another common scheme. Since 1989, the U.S. has used an intricate classification system called the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States. The tariff schedule is the legal resource for determining customs duties or tariff classifications for goods imported into the U.S. The schedule is based on an international standardized system for classifying traded products. “Every good imported into the United States has a classification number that says what it is,” said Whitehurst. “It could be something as simple as an orange or an apple or it could be very complex, depending on the essential characteristics of the item such as what it’s made of and where it’s manufactured.”

Usually importers misclassify goods to lower the duty rate, but that’s not what happened in one instance. In January 2025, CBP officers at the Port of Jacksonville, Florida, did a random cargo inspection and asked the import specialists for their input on a shipment of plastic food containers. “We looked at the shipment and immediately noticed that it was classified as household goods, but the products were coming in large quantities in the thousands. I thought nobody orders a thousand of these little cups for his or her home,” said Heather Janezic, a supervisory import specialist at CBP’s Consumer Products and Mass Merchandising Center.

The shipping documents also revealed that the items were being sold to businesses. “The invoices even included some names of popular fast-food restaurants, which is a clear indicator these shipments were not going to someone’s house,” said Janezic. But the strangest part of the claim was that by classifying the plastic containers as household goods, the company was actually paying a higher duty rate. The duty rate for household plastic containers is 3.4%, while plastic containers imported for commercial use only have a 3% duty.

“It’s very rare to see a company misclassify an imported item with a tariff code that has a higher duty rate than what it would be required to pay. Most companies are trying to save money,” said Janezic. “That’s when we realized that plastic containers manufactured in China for commercial use had an additional 25% duty. If the goods had come from any other country besides China, we would have owed the importer money because the company had overpaid us. But instead, the importer now owed the government an additional $50 million in duties.”

Janezic and her team then looked at other companies that imported the same product from the same manufacturer to see if they were misclassifying the plastic containers too. “We discovered several companies that were,” said Janezic. “But we narrowed it down to four that imported millions of dollars’ worth of merchandise.” The four importers combined owe the U.S. government nearly $39 million. “There are many ways that importers try to evade paying duties including paying a higher duty rate than what is required,” said Janezic. “They find ingenious ways to try to circumvent the system, but in the end, CBP always goes through every possible avenue to collect the revenue that the government is owed.”

Illegal transshipment

Transshipping goods through other countries to disguise the true country of origin is another popular scheme. This is especially the case when importers try to avoid paying duties by shipping goods through countries that have free trade agreements with the U.S. One striking example was discovered in July 2024, when Sonna McWilliams, an import specialist at CBP’s Consumer Products and Mass Merchandising Center, was verifying a free trade agreement claim on a mattress shipment from Singapore. “I looked back six months to a year prior to see the country of origin the importer had been claiming,” said McWilliams. “In the past, the company had claimed China as the country of origin and then all of a sudden it was claiming Singapore.”

McWilliams researched the company and found that it was listed as a Chinese manufacturer. “I suspected the mattresses were transshipped. I didn’t think they were truly from Singapore,” said McWilliams, who was aware that a few years earlier, in December 2019, additional duties were imposed on mattresses manufactured in China because of unfair practices that were undercutting U.S. businesses. To protect U.S. mattress manufacturers, an additional 1731.75% tariff was added to already existing duties. McWilliams asked the company for more information. “I needed proof that the mattresses were actually made in Singapore,” she said.

McWilliams’ suspicions were further confirmed by CBP officers stationed in Singapore. The officers, who are part of CBP’s Container Security Initiative, or CSI, extend the agency’s reach globally. Now operational throughout the world, CSI came out of the aftermath of 9/11. “The idea was to inspect high-risk containers to stop dangerous goods from entering the U.S.,” said Michael Pasko, one of the CBP CSI Singapore officers. “Today, CSI has expanded to more of an all-threats model, which includes financial threats and revenue loss.”

One area the CSI Singapore team focuses on is transshipment. “We know a lot of cargo is transshipped illegally through Singapore,” said Pasko. The country is very well positioned geographically. The Strait of Malacca is a major shipping hub for the world. A lot of feeder ships legally reload containers and consolidate them onto new vessels. But it didn’t make sense for the mattresses to travel west to Singapore from China and then back east to the U.S.” Furthermore, CSI had been tracking the mattress shipments from China. “When the cargo comes in, the mattresses are unloaded. They are stored in a warehouse for a day and then loaded into another container that is shipped to the U.S.,” said Pasko. “The whole process costs anywhere from $1,000 to $3,000 per shipment. There’s no reason to do that unless the importer is trying to hide something.”

From 2014 to 2024, the number of mattress shipments from Singapore to the U.S. catapulted. “The shipments grew exponentially each year. Within a 10-year span, the mattress shipments increased 8,000%. It was mindboggling,” said Pasko. “There’s not a lot of space for manufacturing in Singapore. It’s one of the smallest, most expensive countries in the world. So manufacturing huge, bulky mattresses for a low profit margin just didn’t make sense.”

Pasko went with CBP colleagues to do a site visit at the importer’s manufacturing facility in Singapore. “It was evident that something was definitely wrong. It was clear that the Singapore factory was not manufacturing the mattresses. They were just assembling them,” said Pasko. “We found machinery that looked like it had not been used for a long time and the number of employees could not support the number of mattresses that were being exported from the manufacturer to the United States.”

The information from the site visit was relayed to McWilliams, who denied the importer’s claim for free trade. Instead of paying no duty on the mattress shipments, the importer was required to pay the U.S. government $361.4 million in duties on 483 shipments valued at over $19.4 million.

Building partnerships

CBP works closely with its customs counterparts throughout the world. “Our enforcement is successful because we have these relationships, we work quickly, and we build trust,” said Moreland. An excellent example of this occurred in May 2025, when the Korean Customs Service requested assistance from CBP’s Consumer Products and Mass Merchandising Center to determine if two Korean manufacturers were engaged in trade fraud. “Korean Customs suspected that the manufacturers were exporting jewelry from China and Vietnam to the U.S. and claiming Korea’s free trade agreement,” said Moreland.

Aldie Mayoralgo, an import specialist at the Consumer Products and Mass Merchandising Center, compared documents the Korean government received with those that were presented to CBP. “It was like a giant jigsaw puzzle,” said Mayoralgo. “I was trying to connect A to B to see if an item China sent to Korea was the same item that Korea sent to the United States.” Mayoralgo looked at the weights and descriptions of the items, which were predominantly gold necklaces, bracelets, and rings. “Sometimes it was rather challenging because the documents we received from Korean Customs were written in Chinese or Vietnamese, but the weights of the jewelry were the same.”

Within two months, Mayoralgo provided the information that the Korean Customs Service was seeking. On Aug. 8, 2025, the two Korean manufacturers were arrested for violating the U.S.-Korea Free Trade Agreement. A joint investigation between South Korea and the U.S. revealed that on 187 occasions between April 2021 and April 2025, the two Korean manufacturers had illegally transshipped 1,127 kilograms of Chinese and Vietnamese made jewelry with an estimated value of $53.2 million.

“When most people hear about CBP, they think of officers checking travelers coming from overseas into the country, but just as important is our trade mission, which ensures that imported merchandise is properly described, meets U.S. safety regulations, and that proper duties are paid,” said Moreland. “We do this to make sure that domestic companies are able to compete fairly with foreign competitors selling imported goods. To have the physical security that people commonly think of, we need to have financial security."

It is for this reason that “it’s very important to have this agency continue to enforce and protect the United States’ revenue,” said Whitehurst. “All the revenue that we collect – the duties, the taxes, and the fees —all goes into the U.S. Treasury. It doesn’t go to CBP. It doesn’t go to any one person. It goes to the nation. That’s what we do. We collect revenue for our economic prosperity, security, and to keep our nation safe.”

description:

The sudden expulsion of Haitian TPS holders would have devastating consequences for our nation’s economy.
For example, in health care facilities such as nursing homes, the Haitian work ethic is greatly appreciated even beyond our South Florida community.
And the Senate should join the House in approving a three-year extension for Haitians with TPS.
It’s up to the Senate now to vote “yes” on extending TPS protections for Haitians.
text:
68

The House of Representatives recently passed a bill that would extend TPS (Temporary Protected Status) protections for Haitians for three more years — a critical lifeline for those desperate to avoid returning to the chaos on the island nation, which could be described as a “house on fire.”

This bill — which also needs the Senate’s approval — provides a reprieve to the more than 350,000 Haitians who today live and work legally in the United States under the protection of TPS.

These protections will soon end because the administration has determined, inexplicably, that “country conditions” have improved sufficiently for Haitians in the U.S. to be sent home. Yet Haiti remains a country on the brink.

Troubles in Haiti

Since the disastrous earthquake in 2010, which killed more than 250,000 people in a single day and displaced millions more, the country has faced one calamity after another.

There is widespread gang violence and kidnapping, a rampant cholera epidemic, and spreading food insecurity. The lack of functioning state institutions has resulted in a general breakdown of security, with attacks on women and children becoming commonplace.

It would be an act of abject cruelty for the United States to send families back to such dangerous and unsafe conditions. To do so would only exacerbate Haiti’s ongoing humanitarian crisis.

At the same time, taking advantage of the protections TPS affords, including the opportunity to work legally, these Haitians have already become an integral and contributing part of our society.

Members of the community

Haitians in this country are not “on the dole”; they are not “public charges.” They are hard workers filling jobs that, were it not for them, would go unfilled. The sudden expulsion of Haitian TPS holders would have devastating consequences for our nation’s economy.

For example, in health care facilities such as nursing homes, the Haitian work ethic is greatly appreciated even beyond our South Florida community. In places like Indianapolis and Springfield, Ohio, where Haitians were falsely accused of eating people’s pets, business leaders and a few politicians from both parties have said that losing the Haitians would hurt the local economy.

Of course, some would argue that “temporary” should mean temporary. I cannot disagree. TPS was passed by Congress in the 1990s because lawmakers saw it as a solution for those who found themselves in the U.S. but who, because of conditions in their countries of origin, could not return home safely.

It has turned out to be, admittedly, an imperfect tool — and one that cannot substitute for the hard work of immigration reform that Congress has to undertake sooner or later. But without any other workable alternative, TPS is what’s available. And the Senate should join the House in approving a three-year extension for Haitians with TPS.

As I said, this would give Haitians a reprieve, albeit a temporary one; and, at the same time, three years could give our lawmakers time to explore more durable, more workable solutions. This certainly is a better course of action than pulling the floor out from under families without any workable alternative. And, to be sure, the mass deportation of 350,000 men, women and their children to a country in dire straits is not a workable alternative.

Every single day, I see the human consequences of often unintended public policy decisions that result in chronic uncertainty, fear, and the disruption of families and entire communities. It’s up to the Senate now to vote “yes” on extending TPS protections for Haitians.

Archbishop Thomas G. Wenski leads the Archdiocese of Miami.

text:
A federal judge dealt a far-reaching blow to a Trump administration policy of arresting immigrants at immigration court, ruling Tuesday that the practice has to stop in every kind of courthouse across the nation.

The ruling in the Northern District of California by Judge P. Casey Pitts of San Jose goes beyond what even some of the Bay Area plaintiffs who sued the administration anticipated in December, when the same judge temporarily blocked immigration courthouse arrests in Northern California. At the time, the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights, American Civil Liberties Union and their immigrant clients were asking for the order to apply nationwide.

But, as Judge Pitts explained in a footnote, he was moved to deliver a more expansive order based, in part, on the Trump administration’s policy ineptitude.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

There was “no clear way to vacate only the portion of those policies that impacts immigration courthouses,” Pitts wrote, “because ICE’s interim 2025 courthouse-arrest policy rescinds … prior restrictions on enforcement actions at both immigration and non-immigration courthouses in one fell swoop.”

Breaking with four decades of federal policy, the White House had greenlit arrests inside immigration courthouses last year following a pressure campaign by President Donald Trump and senior adviser Stephen Miller to massively increase detention and deportations.

San Francisco Chronicle Logo

See more S.F. Chronicle on Google

Make us a Preferred Source to get more of our news when you search.

Add Preferred Source

San Francisco was an epicenter of the arrests and of a legal campaign to halt them. Two of five federal lawsuits originated here.

The Lawyers’ Committee filed a class-action lawsuit challenging the practice in September, arguing that it violated the Administrative Procedures Act, a federal statute governing how agencies set policy for 80 years.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Concluding that Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Justice’s Executive Office for Immigration Review had “contravened” the Administrative Procedures Act’s “reasoned-decisionmaking requirement,” Pitts vacated the administration’s courthouse-arrests policy and also a waiver it had granted itself to detain immigrants in ICE field offices for more than 12 hours, finding the practice “unconstitutional.”

Citing sanctuary cities’ lack of cooperation with its deportation agenda, the Trump administration dispensed with a decades-old compact against immigration courthouse arrests through two policy memos that claimed agents would prioritize criminals, gang members and terrorists and that dismissed the chilling effect the arrests would have on immigrants deciding whether to show up for court.

But the practice immediately swept up immigrants who had been allowed into the country to pursue asylum claims and other forms of legal status and were complying with their requirements under immigration law, such as the three plaintiffs who challenged the policy in the Bay Area.

Carmen Aracely Pablo Sequen, an abuse survivor from Guatemala with a pending asylum application, had exited a routine immigration hearing in July 2025 when three ICE agents surrounded the local bakery worker and hustled her to a holding area.

Something similar happened to Ligia Garcia, an asylum applicant from Columbia, when she left her September 2025 hearing at the immigration court on Sansome Street.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

After ICE nearly separated her from her infant daughter at the San Francisco Immigration Court in September 2025, Yulisa Alvarado Ambrocio joined the other plaintiffs in the Lawyers’ Committee suit.

Civil immigrant detention is reserved for the purposes of ensuring attendance at immigration proceedings and requires a reason to redetain someone who was previously released.

“For 40 years, ICE had a policy of not redetaining someone after they had released them unless something materially changed. They missed a hearing, they had some kind of serious criminal misconduct that changed the game,” said Bree Bernwanger, senior staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union Foundation of Northern California and a co-counsel in a different San Francisco-set courthouse arrests case.

The government contended the judge lacked jurisdiction to hear the case and asked for a stay pending appeal. But the federal government was forced into an embarrassing admission that it misinterpreted its own attempts to rescind the policies, and that they didn’t apply to immigration courthouses after all.

Now, the Trump administration can either appeal the ruling to the Ninth Circuit or make another attempt at drafting immigration enforcement policies that comply with the APA.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Pitts rejected the government’s request to pause the case during appeal, writing that a final ruling by the Ninth Circuit could be more than a year away.

The judge was at times scathing in his 71-page ruling, opening with, “For 80 years, Congress has commanded federal agencies to think before they act.”

“The courthouse is meant to be a refuge for the pursuit of justice, not a hunting ground for ICE,” Jordan Wells, senior staff attorney at the Bay Area chapter of the Lawyers’ Committee, said in a statement. “No one, including immigrants, should be forced to choose between their liberty and their day in court.”

text:
Eight people who US prosecutors say have ties to Antifa have collectively been sentenced to 450 years in prison for their roles in a riot outside an immigration detention centre in Texas.

A former US Marine Corps reservist, who was convicted of attempted murder of a law enforcement officer, was sentenced to 100 years in prison. The others' sentences range between 30 to 70 years, according to the justice department.

A US judge called their actions on 4 July "an assault on democracy", while their families condemned the length of their sentences.

"The sentences handed down today make clear that Antifa terrorists who attack law enforcement and federal facilities will face swift and uncompromising justice," Acting US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement, condemning violent extremism.

The US Department of Justice (DOJ) said the North Texas Antifa Cell operatives began shooting off and throwing fireworks at the facility in Prairieland, just south of Dallas, on the Independence Day holiday last summer, as well as vandalising vehicles and a guard kiosk on the property.

The eight were convicted on an array of charges, including rioting, using weapons and explosives, providing material support to terrorists, and obstruction.

Benjamin Hanil Song, the purported leader of the group, was sentenced to 100 years in prison. According to the justice department, he had faced a minimum penalty of 20 years.

Song said in a written statement on Tuesday that he fired his gun because he believed the police officer was preparing to shoot a protester, according to multiple media outlets and an advocacy group for the defendants.

His mother Hope Song has disputed claims that he shot the officer and said he didn't intend to hurt anyone, according to the Associated Press.

Maricela Rueda was sentenced to 70 years in prison; Cameron Arnold (also known as Autumn Hill), Savanna Batten, Zachary Evetts, Bradford Morris (also known as Meagan Morris) and Elizabeth Soto were each sentenced to 50 years in prison; and Daniel Rolando Sanchez-Estrada was sentenced to 30 years in prison.

A ninth defendant, Ines Soto, will be sentenced on 1 July. Seven others involved in the incident pleaded guilty before the trial to one count of providing material support to terrorists. They will also be sentenced on 1 July.

In a statement on Tuesday, the DOJ said the North Texas Antifa Cell was part of a network of individuals and small groups ascribing to an ideology that calls for the overthrow of the US government, law enforcement and the system of law.

While other immigration facilities have seen numerous protests, as well as visits from Democratic lawmakers, the Prairieland site had been relatively free of disruptions.

Some of the protest's attendees said they believed that night was supposed to be a "noise demonstration" that did not include violence.

The defendants have denied any affiliation with Antifa and have said they attended the demonstration to support detained immigrants.

Antifa has long been a target for Trump. In September he signed an executive order designating the loosely organised, far-left movement as a domestic terror organisation.

text:
(CN) — A federal judge blocked Tuesday a new set of policies implemented by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including the new practice of arresting noncitizens at immigration courthouses, because the agency didn’t go through the proper rulemaking process.

“For 80 years, Congress has commanded federal agencies to think before they act,” U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts, a Joe Biden appointee, wrote in his 71-page ruling. The Administrative Procedure Act, he added, “demands that an agency at least provide sound reasons for following its chosen course” — which, he found, the Justice Department and ICE didn’t do.

“It is now clear that the lack of connection between ICE’s stated rationales for the 2025 courthouse-arrest policies and the expansion of arrests at immigration courthouses results not from merely unreasoned decision-making but a complete lack of decision-making,” Pitts wrote.

Plaintiffs’ attorney Nisha Kashyap, the program director for the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights in San Francisco, called the nationwide ruling “tremendously significant.”

“The Trump administration has turned immigration courts into hunting grounds,” Kashyap said in a phone interview. “This order vacates the policy that allowed for those mass arrests.”

In the years between 2014 and 2025, it was ICE policy to only arrest noncitizens at courthouses who were high-risk, like those already convicted of a crime or who were suspected of being terrorists, spies or members of criminal gangs. In 2021, ICE further restricted itself to enforcement actions only against individuals who presented a national security threat or an immediate risk of destroying evidence.

That abruptly changed after President Donald Trump was inaugurated for a second time. In May 2025, ICE and the DOJ adopted a new policy, allowing for civil enforcement actions whenever “credible information … leads them to believe” that the noncitizen they seek to arrest “will be present” at a courthouse. Though the policy did not mention immigration courts specifically, in practice, agents targeted those courthouses. One immigration judge has said in a declaration that she “noticed a dramatic decline in attendance at master calendar hearings in [her] courtroom," thanks to increased ICE presence in her court.

Carmen Aracely Pablo Sequen, an asylum-seeker from Guatemala, sued the federal government in August after she was arrested while leaving a routine hearing at the San Francisco immigration court and then detained. Two others were later added in an amended complaint. The three plaintiffs challenged the new ICE policy of making arrests at immigration courts and other new Trump-era practices, like the waiving of what was once a 12-hour limit on detention in short-term holding facilities. The plaintiffs also accused ICE of depriving detainees in a holding facility in San Francisco of “adequate hygiene and sanitation, sleep, medical care and access to counsel.” The plaintiffs also sought class action status, which Pitts approved on Tuesday.

Pitts had previously rejected the government’s motion to dismiss the lawsuit and had also granted a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction requiring Pablo Sequen’s immediate release and “enjoining the government from re-detaining her absent prior notice and a hearing before an immigration judge at which the government demonstrated a valid basis for her detention.” The government has appealed the preliminary injunction, an appeal that is still pending.

On Tuesday, Pitts ruled in favor of the plaintiffs’ motion for summary judgment and invalidated “courthouse-arrest policies and ICE’s 12-hour-detention waiver” under the Administrative Procedure Act. He called the courthouse-arrest policies “an irrational departure” from the 2021 rules and said they “failed to display a conscious awareness that [they were] rescinding an arrest policy applicable to immigration courts.”

“The government spent more than six months arguing to this court that ICE’s 2025 courthouse-arrest policies represented an intentional and reasoned choice to expand arrests at immigration courthouses,” Pitts wrote. “The argument was unconvincing.”

While the government pointed out that law enforcement agencies routinely arrest suspects at courthouses, Pitts found the analogy didn’t apply since ICE “is not arresting individuals who appear for criminal or civil violations ‘unrelated’ to the arrest but instead arresting noncitizens based on the very immigration offenses for which the noncitizens are appearing in immigration court.”

The government had also cited a need to “reduce public safety risks,” but, Pitts wrote, it had failed “to explain how public safety is improved by unfettered arrests at immigration courthouses of the many noncitizens whom ICE has determined do not endanger public safety.”

As to detaining people in short-term holding facilities for days on end, Pitts wrote that ICE had failed to consider the agency’s “obligation under the Fifth Amendment not to subject civil immigration detainees to punitive conditions of confinement.”

The Pablo Sequen case remains active as to a few other constitutional claims relating to the conditions of confinement in the San Francisco holding facility. Similar lawsuits have been filed in other jurisdictions, including Baltimore, Chicago and Minnesota. Plaintiffs in a lawsuit in New York also challenged courthouse arrest policies in that state.
